practice: Conduct all data validation on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Identify all data sources and classify them into trusted and untrusted. Validate all data from untrusted sources (e.g., Databases, file streams, etc.)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: There should be a centralized input validation routine for the application
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Specify proper character sets, such as UTF-8, for all sources of input
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Encode data to a common character set before validating (Canonicalize)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All validation failures should result in input rejection
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Determine if the system supports UTF-8 extended character sets and if so, validate after UTF-8 decoding is completed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate all client provided data before processing, including all parameters, URLs and HTTP header content (e.g. Cookie names and values). Be sure to include automated post backs from JavaScript, Flash or other embedded code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Verify that header values in both requests and responses contain only ASCII characters
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate data from redirects (An attacker may submit malicious content directly to the target of the redirect, thus circumventing application logic and any validation performed before the redirect)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate for expected data types
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate data range
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate data length
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate all input against a "white" list of allowed characters, whenever possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If any potentially hazardous characters must be allowed as input, be sure that you implement additional controls like output encoding, secure task specific APIs and accounting for the utilization of that data throughout the application . Examples of common hazardous characters include: < > " ' % ( ) & + \ \' \"
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If your standard validation routine cannot address the following inputs, then they should be checked discretely – Check for null bytes (%00) – Check for new line characters (%0d, %0a, \r, \n) – Check for “dot-dot-slash" (../ or ..\) path alterations characters. In cases where UTF-8 extended character set encoding is supported, address alternate representation like: %c0%ae%c0%ae/ (Utilize canonicalization to address double encoding or other forms of obfuscation attacks)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Conduct all encoding on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize a standard, tested routine for each type of outbound encoding
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Contextually output encode all data returned to the client that originated outside the application's trust boundary. HTML entity encoding is one example, but does not work in all cases
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Encode all characters unless they are known to be safe for the intended interpreter
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Contextually sanitize all output of un-trusted data to queries for SQL, XML, and LDAP
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Sanitize all output of un-trusted data to operating system commands
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Require authentication for all pages and resources, except those specifically intended to be public
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All authentication controls must be enforced on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Establish and utilize standard, tested, authentication services whenever possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use a centralized implementation for all authentication controls, including libraries that call external authentication services
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Segregate authentication logic from the resource being requested and use redirection to and from the centralized authentication control
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All authentication controls should fail securely
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All administrative and account management functions must be at least as secure as the primary authentication mechanism
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If your application manages a credential store, it should ensure that only cryptographically strong one-way salted hashes of passwords are stored and that the table/file that stores the passwords and keys is write-able only by the application. (Do not use the MD5 algorithm if it can be avoided)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Password hashing must be implemented on a trusted system (e.g., The server).
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate the authentication data only on completion of all data input, especially for sequential authentication implementations
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Authentication failure responses should not indicate which part of the authentication data was incorrect. For example, instead of "Invalid username" or "Invalid password", just use "Invalid username and/or password" for both. Error responses must be truly identical in both display and source code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize authentication for connections to external systems that involve sensitive information or functions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Authentication credentials for accessing services external to the application should be encrypted and stored in a protected location on a trusted system (e.g., The server). The source code is NOT a secure location
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use only HTTP POST requests to transmit authentication credentials
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Only send non-temporary passwords over an encrypted connection or as encrypted data, such as in an encrypted email. Temporary passwords associated with email resets may be an exception
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce password complexity requirements established by policy or regulation. Authentication credentials should be sufficient to withstand attacks that are typical of the threats in the deployed environment. (e.g., requiring the use of alphabetic as well as numeric and/or special characters)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce password length requirements established by policy or regulation. Eight characters is commonly used, but 16 is better or consider the use of multi-word pass phrases
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Password entry should be obscured on the user's screen. (e.g., on web forms use the input type "password")
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce account disabling after an established number of invalid login attempts (e.g., five attempts is common). The account must be disabled for a period of time sufficient to discourage brute force guessing of credentials, but not so long as to allow for a denial-of-service attack to be performed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Password reset and changing operations require the same level of controls as account creation and authentication.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Password reset questions should support sufficiently random answers. (e.g., "favorite book" is a bad question because “The Bible” is a very common answer)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If using email based resets, only send email to a pre-registered address with a temporary link/password
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Temporary passwords and links should have a short expiration time
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce the changing of temporary passwords on the next use
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Notify users when a password reset occurs
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Prevent password re-use
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Passwords should be at least one day old before they can be changed, to prevent attacks on password re-use
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce password changes based on requirements established in policy or regulation. Critical systems may require more frequent changes. The time between resets must be administratively controlled
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disable "remember me" functionality for password fields
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The last use (successful or unsuccessful) of a user account should be reported to the user at their next successful login
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement monitoring to identify attacks against multiple user accounts, utilizing the same password. This attack pattern is used to bypass standard lockouts, when user IDs can be harvested or guessed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Change all vendor-supplied default passwords and user IDs or disable the associated accounts
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Re-authenticate users prior to performing critical operations
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use Multi-Factor Authentication for highly sensitive or high value transactional accounts
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If using third party code for authentication, inspect the code carefully to ensure it is not affected by any malicious code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use the server or framework’s session management controls. The application should only recognize these session identifiers as valid
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Session identifier creation must always be done on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Session management controls should use well vetted algorithms that ensure sufficiently random session identifiers
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Set the domain and path for cookies containing authenticated session identifiers to an appropriately restricted value for the site
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Logout functionality should fully terminate the associated session or connection
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Logout functionality should be available from all pages protected by authorization
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Establish a session inactivity timeout that is as short as possible, based on balancing risk and business functional requirements. In most cases it should be no more than several hours
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disallow persistent logins and enforce periodic session terminations, even when the session is active. Especially for applications supporting rich network connections or connecting to critical systems. Termination times should support business requirements and the user should receive sufficient notification to mitigate negative impacts
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If a session was established before login, close that session and establish a new session after a successful login
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Generate a new session identifier on any re-authentication
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not allow concurrent logins with the same user ID
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not expose session identifiers in URLs, error messages or logs. Session identifiers should only be located in the HTTP cookie header. For example, do not pass session identifiers as GET parameters
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Protect server side session data from unauthorized access, by other users of the server, by implementing appropriate access controls on the server
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Generate a new session identifier and deactivate the old one periodically. (This can mitigate certain session hijacking scenarios where the original identifier was compromised)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Generate a new session identifier if the connection security changes from HTTP to HTTPS, as can occur during authentication. Within an application, it is recommended to consistently utilize HTTPS rather than switching between HTTP to HTTPS.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Supplement standard session management for sensitive server-side operations, like account manage- ment, by utilizing per-session strong random tokens or parameters. This method can be used to prevent Cross Site Request Forgery attacks
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Supplement standard session management for highly sensitive or critical operations by utilizing per-request, as opposed to per-session, strong random tokens or parameters
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Set the "secure" attribute for cookies transmitted over an TLS connection
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Set cookies with the HttpOnly attribute, unless you specifically require client-side scripts within your application to read or set a cookie's value
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use only trusted system objects, e.g. server side session objects, for making access authorization decisions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use a single site-wide component to check access authorization. This includes libraries that call external authorization services
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Access controls should fail securely
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Deny all access if the application cannot access its security configuration information
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce authorization controls on every request, including those made by server side scripts, "includes" and requests from rich client-side technologies like AJAX and Flash
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Segregate privileged logic from other application code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to files or other resources, including those outside the application's direct control, to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to protected URLs to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to protected functions to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict direct object references to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to services to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to application data to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to user and data attributes and policy information used by access controls
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access security-relevant configuration information to only authorized users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Server side implementation and presentation layer representations of access control rules must match
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If state data must be stored on the client, use encryption and integrity checking on the server side to catch state tampering.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Enforce application logic flows to comply with business rules
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Limit the number of transactions a single user or device can perform in a given period of time. The transactions/time should be above the actual business requirement, but low enough to deter automated attacks
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use the "referer" header as a supplemental check only, it should never be the sole authorization check, as it is can be spoofed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If long authenticated sessions are allowed, periodically re-validate a user’s authorization to ensure that their privileges have not changed and if they have, log the user out and force them to re-authenticate
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement account auditing and enforce the disabling of unused accounts (e.g., After no more than 30 days from the expiration of an account’s password.)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The application must support disabling of accounts and terminating sessions when authorization ceases (e.g., Changes to role, employment status, business process, etc.)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Service accounts or accounts supporting connections to or from external systems should have the least privilege possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Create an Access Control Policy to document an application's business rules, data types and access authorization criteria and/or processes so that access can be properly provisioned and controlled. This includes identifying access requirements for both the data and system resources
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All cryptographic functions used to protect secrets from the application user must be implemented on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Protect master secrets from unauthorized access
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Cryptographic modules should fail securely
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All random numbers, random file names, random GUIDs, and random strings should be generated using the cryptographic module’s approved random number generator when these random values are intended to be un-guessable
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Cryptographic modules used by the application should be compliant to FIPS 140-2 or an equivalent standard. (See http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/STM/cmvp/validation.html)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Establish and utilize a policy and process for how cryptographic keys will be managed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not disclose sensitive information in error responses, including system details, session identifiers or account information
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use error handlers that do not display debugging or stack trace information
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement generic error messages and use custom error pages
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The application should handle application errors and not rely on the server configuration
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Properly free allocated memory when error conditions occur
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Error handling logic associated with security controls should deny access by default
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: All logging controls should be implemented on a trusted system (e.g., The server)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Logging controls should support both success and failure of specified security events
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure logs contain important log event data
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure log entries that include un-trusted data will not execute as code in the intended log viewing interface or software
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict access to logs to only authorized individuals
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize a master routine for all logging operations
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not store sensitive information in logs, including unnecessary system details, session identifiers or passwords
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure that a mechanism exists to conduct log analysis
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all input validation failures
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all authentication attempts, especially failures
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all access control failures
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all apparent tampering events, including unexpected changes to state data
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log attempts to connect with invalid or expired session tokens
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all system exceptions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all administrative functions, including changes to the security configuration settings
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log all backend TLS connection failures
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Log cryptographic module failures
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use a cryptographic hash function to validate log entry integrity
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement least privilege, restrict users to only the functionality, data and system information that is required to perform their tasks
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Protect all cached or temporary copies of sensitive data stored on the server from unauthorized access and purge those temporary working files a soon as they are no longer required.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Encrypt highly sensitive stored information, like authentication verification data, even on the server side. Always use well vetted algorithms, see "Cryptographic Practices" for additional guidance
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Protect server-side source-code from being downloaded by a user
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not store passwords, connection strings or other sensitive information in clear text or in any non-cryptographically secure manner on the client side. This includes embedding in insecure formats like: MS viewstate, Adobe flash or compiled code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove comments in user accessible production code that may reveal backend system or other sensitive information
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove unnecessary application and system documentation as this can reveal useful information to attackers
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not include sensitive information in HTTP GET request parameters
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disable auto complete features on forms expected to contain sensitive information, including authen- tication
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disable client side caching on pages containing sensitive information. Cache-Control: no-store, may be used in conjunction with the HTTP header control "Pragma: no-cache", which is less effective, but is HTTP/1.0 backward compatible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The application should support the removal of sensitive data when that data is no longer required. (e.g. personal information or certain financial data)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement appropriate access controls for sensitive data stored on the server. This includes cached data, temporary files and data that should be accessible only by specific system users
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement encryption for the transmission of all sensitive information. This should include TLS for protecting the connection and may be supplemented by discrete encryption of sensitive files or non-HTTP based connections
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: TLS certificates should be valid and have the correct domain name, not be expired, and be installed with intermediate certificates when required
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Failed TLS connections should not fall back to an insecure connection
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize TLS connections for all content requiring authenticated access and for all other sensitive information
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize TLS for connections to external systems that involve sensitive information or functions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize a single standard TLS implementation that is configured appropriately
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Specify character encodings for all connections
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Filter parameters containing sensitive information from the HTTP referer, when linking to external sites
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure servers, frameworks and system components are running the latest approved version
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure servers, frameworks and system components have all patches issued for the version in use
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Turn off directory listings
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict the web server, process and service accounts to the least privileges possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: When exceptions occur, fail securely
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove all unnecessary functionality and files
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove test code or any functionality not intended for production, prior to deployment
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Prevent disclosure of your directory structure in the robots.txt file by placing directories not intended for public indexing into an isolated parent directory. Then "Disallow" that entire parent directory in the robots.txt file rather than Disallowing each individual directory
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Define which HTTP methods, Get or Post, the application will support and whether it will be handled differently in different pages in the application
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disable unnecessary HTTP methods, such as WebDAV extensions. If an extended HTTP method that supports file handling is required, utilize a well-vetted authentication mechanism
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: If the web server handles both HTTP 1.0 and 1.1, ensure that both are configured in a similar manor or insure that you understand any difference that may exist (e.g. handling of extended HTTP methods)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove unnecessary information from HTTP response headers related to the OS, web-server version and application frameworks
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The security configuration store for the application should be able to be output in human readable form to support auditing
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement an asset management system and register system components and software in it
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Isolate development environments from the production network and provide access only to authorized development and test groups. Development environments are often configured less securely than production environments and attackers may use this difference to discover shared weaknesses or as an avenue for exploitation
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement a software change control system to manage and record changes to the code both in development and production
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use strongly typed parameterized queries
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize input validation and output encoding and be sure to address meta characters. If these fail, do not run the database command
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure that variables are strongly typed
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The application should use the lowest possible level of privilege when accessing the database
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use secure credentials for database access
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Connection strings should not be hard coded within the application. Connection strings should be stored in a separate configuration file on a trusted system and they should be encrypted.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use stored procedures to abstract data access and allow for the removal of permissions to the base tables in the database
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Close the connection as soon as possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove or change all default database administrative passwords. Utilize strong passwords/phrases or implement multi-factor authentication
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Turn off all unnecessary database functionality (e.g., unnecessary stored procedures or services, utility packages, install only the minimum set of features and options required (surface area reduction))
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Remove unnecessary default vendor content (e.g., sample schemas)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Disable any default accounts that are not required to support business requirements
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: The application should connect to the database with different credentials for every trust distinction (e.g., user, read-only user, guest, administrators)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not pass user supplied data directly to any dynamic include function
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Require authentication before allowing a file to be uploaded
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Limit the type of files that can be uploaded to only those types that are needed for business purposes
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Validate uploaded files are the expected type by checking file headers. Checking for file type by extension alone is not sufficient
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not save files in the same web context as the application. Files should either go to the content server or in the database.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Prevent or restrict the uploading of any file that may be interpreted by the web server.
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Turn off execution privileges on file upload directories
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement safe uploading in UNIX by mounting the targeted file directory as a logical drive using the associated path or the chrooted environment
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: When referencing existing files, use a white list of allowed file names and types. Validate the value of the parameter being passed and if it does not match one of the expected values, either reject it or use a hard coded default file value for the content instead
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not pass user supplied data into a dynamic redirect. If this must be allowed, then the redirect should accept only validated, relative path URLs
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not pass directory or file paths, use index values mapped to pre-defined list of paths
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Never send the absolute file path to the client
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Ensure application files and resources are read-only
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Scan user uploaded files for viruses and malware
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize input and output control for un-trusted data
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Double check that the buffer is as large as specified
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: When using functions that accept a number of bytes to copy, such as strncpy(), be aware that if the destination buffer size is equal to the source buffer size, it may not NULL-terminate the string
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Check buffer boundaries if calling the function in a loop and make sure there is no danger of writing past the allocated space
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Truncate all input strings to a reasonable length before passing them to the copy and concatenation functions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Specifically close resources, don’t rely on garbage collection. (e.g., connection objects, file handles, etc.)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use non-executable stacks when available
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Avoid the use of known vulnerable functions (e.g., printf, strcat, strcpy etc.)
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Properly free allocated memory upon the completion of functions and at all exit points
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use tested and approved managed code rather than creating new unmanaged code for common tasks
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize task specific built-in APIs to conduct operating system tasks. Do not allow the application to issue commands directly to the Operating System, especially through the use of application initiated command shells
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Use checksums or hashes to verify the integrity of interpreted code, libraries, executables, and configuration files
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Utilize locking to prevent multiple simultaneous requests or use a synchronization mechanism to prevent race conditions
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Protect shared variables and resources from inappropriate concurrent access
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Explicitly initialize all your variables and other data stores, either during declaration or just before the first usage
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: In cases where the application must run with elevated privileges, raise privileges as late as possible, and drop them as soon as possible
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Avoid calculation errors by understanding your programming language's underlying representation and how it interacts with numeric calculation. Pay close attention to byte size discrepancies, precision, signed/unsigned distinctions, truncation, conversion and casting between types, "not-a- number" calculations, and how your language handles numbers that are too large or too small for its underlying representation
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Do not pass user supplied data to any dynamic execution function
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Restrict users from generating new code or altering existing code
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Review all secondary applications, third party code and libraries to determine business necessity and validate safe functionality, as these can introduce new vulnerabilities
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide

practice: Implement safe updating. If the application will utilize automatic updates, then use cryptographic signatures for your code and ensure your download clients verify those signatures. Use encrypted channels to transfer the code from the host server
source: OWASP Secure Coding Practices - Quick Reference Guide
